prompt.context: A cable TV company from Canada, World View, had recently entered the US market in the northeast to expand its market share. World View saw this move as an opportunity to capture a large part of the US market (4MM consumers) in a market with very little competition.
prompt.question: However, in the last couple of years, much to the surprise of management, World View has been unable to make a profit. You have been hired to figure out why and advise them on their next move.

clarifying_info.q: Did World View incur additional costs per customer in the new market compared to Canada?
clarifying_info.a: No. Based on the potential number of subscribers, they have instituted the same system that was in place. Costs associated with cable wire, debt, maintenance costs, etc. are all proportionally the same.

clarifying_info.q: How many subscribers does World View currently have out of the 4MM potential customers?
Are other cable companies capturing the remaining market?
clarifying_info.a: No, competition is not an issue. Those that have not been acquired as customers simply do not have cable.

clarifying_info.q: How is the consumer in the northeast US different from the one in Canada in terms of viewing behavior?
clarifying_info.a: The Canadian consumer does not rely much on local stations for watching TV; cable is a major source of entertainment and news coverage. In the northeast US, consumers tend to shy away from paying $40 a month and settle for watching local stations.

clarifying_info.q: Does the new market have a lower income level?
How many local stations are there and do they meet most of the needs of consumers?
clarifying_info.a: There are about 16 local stations that have coverage over the entire northeast. They provide programming that the consumer wants, and the average consumer in the northeast watches regular TV more than cable compared with the Canadian consumer.

clarifying_info.q: Do local stations have good reception and how much do they charge?
clarifying_info.a: They have very good reception and are part of basic TV, so they are free.

clarifying_info.q: Is World View providing programming that local stations are not?
clarifying_info.a: Some, but consumers don't seem to be interested. They don't feel that it's worth $40.

framework: Use the profitability framework: analyze both revenue and cost sides
Examine revenue: number of subscribers vs. total potential market, and pricing
Examine costs: are costs per customer in line with Canada?
Analyze the consumer: viewing habits, income levels, and willingness to pay in northeast US vs. Canada
Analyze competition and substitutes: other cable providers and free local TV stations
Identify structural differences between the Canadian market and the northeast US market

questions.prompt: Why is World View unable to make a profit despite entering a seemingly uncompetitive market?
questions.guidance: A strong answer identifies that the core problem is insufficient subscribers (2.1MM out of 4MM potential). Costs are in line with Canada, so the problem is on the revenue/demand side. The candidate should probe consumer behavior and alternatives, discovering that free local TV (16 stations, good reception) serves northeast US consumers well, making them unwilling to pay $40/month for cable. Lower income (~20% below Canada) compounds the low willingness-to-pay. Competition is not from other cable companies but from free over-the-air local TV as a substitute.

questions.prompt: What are the key differences between World View's Canadian customer base and its northeast US customer base?
questions.guidance: Canada: heavy reliance on cable as primary entertainment and news source; consumers willing to pay $40/month. Northeast US: 16 free local stations with full regional coverage and good reception; consumers satisfied with free TV; average income roughly 20% lower; consumers do not perceive sufficient incremental value in cable at $40/month.

brainstorming.prompt: What strategic options does World View have to improve its position in the northeast US market?

categories.name: Pricing & Packaging
ideas: Introduce a smaller, cheaper cable package targeting consumers who want only a few cable channels
Offer promotional or introductory pricing to lower the trial barrier
Tiered pricing: basic cable tier at a price point competitive with perceived value vs. free TV

categories.name: Consumer Education & Marketing
ideas: Educate consumers on unique programming not available on local stations
Highlight HD quality, on-demand content, or exclusive sports/events
Targeted campaigns in higher-income sub-regions of the northeast

categories.name: Geographic Focus
ideas: Scale back operations to specific sub-regions where cable uptake is higher
Focus on urban areas with higher income and greater appetite for premium content

categories.name: Exit
ideas: If none of the above strategies can restore profitability, exit the northeast US market
Redeploy capital to other expansion opportunities with more favorable consumer profiles

recommendation: World View is unprofitable because it captured only 2.1MM of 4MM potential subscribers; the remaining consumers are not choosing competitors but are simply satisfied with 16 free local stations that meet their entertainment needs at zero cost. Combined with a 20% lower average income vs. Canada, consumers do not perceive $40/month cable as worthwhile.

World View should restructure its offering: introduce a lower-priced, smaller channel package to increase subscriber penetration and test consumer response, while scaling back operations to the most promising sub-regions.
risks: Pricing down may compress margins further if subscriber gains do not offset revenue-per-user decline
Consumer preferences in the northeast may be structurally resistant to cable adoption regardless of price
Continued losses during a turnaround period could strain the Canadian parent balance sheet
next_steps: Design and pilot a reduced-package offering at a lower price point in a test sub-region
Run a targeted consumer education campaign emphasizing exclusive content and value
Set clear profitability milestones; if unmet within a defined timeframe, initiate market exit planning
